Matt worked on **JP Morgan Chase’s** ACCESS Next Generation payments platform from **August 2009 to June 2012**, serving as Technology Delivery Lead. The bank’s treasury operations depended on separate regional systems, while Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform needed substantial custom engineering to meet its requirements. Payment types had different formatting, validation, compliance, and approval workflows, all under aggressive delivery timelines.

Matt managed a blended team of **40+** **Accenture** and bank resources across Mumbai, Bangalore, and the US. He spent **70 to 80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices, working through where the platform’s native capabilities ended and bank-specific development was required.

He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and tax payment modules, plus Message Authentication Code security so corporate users could verify payment integrity before release. Contextual help explained wire fields, tax codes, and FX requirements directly within payment workflows. He also delivered the centralized payments gateway, handling message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12 countries**.

For corporate client administrators, Matt replaced tedious individual permission configuration with role-based access controls, bulk changes, and a centralized dashboard. Entitlement management dropped from **days to minutes**. He also led payments data migration, preserving client configurations, entitlement structures, and transaction histories without disrupting live payment operations.

Regional rollout required different data visibility and access rules. Matt translated jurisdiction-specific requirements into platform configuration and sequenced launches by regulatory readiness, enabling rollout across APAC, EMEA, and the Americas without regulatory blockers.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, serving **135,000+ clients across 180+ countries**. Corporate treasurers gained a single portal for payments and cash visibility instead of separate regional logins. Matt also owned production incident response, coordinating root-cause analysis and live status updates across bank, offshore, and vendor teams.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt describes his leadership philosophy.

Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose. He describes engineering teams he inherited as “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” At **Accenture**, his focus was on removing those barriers, not adding more process: making intent explicit, building psychological safety, and pushing decisions to the people closest to the work.

He uses transparency, direct feedback, and open communication. He coaches teams to think clearly, not just execute tasks, and grounds engineering culture in automation, continuous delivery, and quality-first practices. At the Cloud Innovation Center, teams accelerated delivery **4x** once they embraced lean product and modern engineering practices. In his words, “It didn’t happen overnight, but it stuck.”

His “permit to fail” environment has specific practices behind it. When teams avoided risks because they feared blame, Matt organized non-punitive post-mortems and supported lean, low-stakes experiments with structured hypotheses and controlled iterations. Teams applied lessons to subsequent sprints to prevent recurring failures. In product incubation, he set expectations that early prototypes and user tests would likely fail intentionally, then used user research, JTBD framing, and rapid testing to shape product direction week by week.

He also brings Product, Engineering, and Design together in balanced teams with equal participation and shared accountability. Rather than preserving role silos and handoffs, he embedded pair programming, collaborative coding, retrospectives, and autonomous workflow changes. Those teams reduced project delays and achieved **zero-defect production code** through iterative development and real-time feedback loops.

Matt’s work centers on Execution & Delivery, Org & Working-Model Transformation, and Talent & Enablement. He builds new capabilities: products, platforms, and teams that last beyond the engagement. His career runs from software engineer to solution architect to director and Cloud Innovation Center leader.

At **Accenture**, clients needed to move beyond waterfall delivery, feature factories, and siloed teams. Matt built the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers from **0 to 150+ practitioners**, with full P&L accountability. He brought product managers, designers, and engineers together in balanced teams, embedded pair programming, test-driven development, and automated pipelines, and adapted those practices for enterprise security, compliance, and legacy systems. Practitioners progressed through an “I do, we do, you do” learning model. The centers delivered **30+ product engagements** across **15+ Fortune 500 clients**, achieving **4X faster velocity** and zero-defect deployments. Delivery excellence and client relationships generated **\$100M+ in repeat business**.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, regional leaders competing over requirements put a global Salesforce rollout at risk of fragmenting into separate regional projects. Brought in to stabilize delivery, Matt negotiated priorities across APAC, EMEA, and the Americas, created a shared backlog, and coordinated dependencies across **7 workstreams**. The platform launched on schedule across **12 countries** for **1,200 users**, with no mid-flight scope renegotiations.

At **Norfolk Southern**, rising defects contradicted near-complete test coverage. Matt took ownership in front of the client and account leadership rather than defending the dashboard. He audited the code and tests, rebuilt vague backlog stories, and brought TDD experts alongside engineers for hands-on coaching. Defect rates dropped, and the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see.

🐾 Here’s a time Matt failed, with consequences for both customers and a teammate.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases. Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup, but he relied on the existing documentation instead of verifying that the controls were correct.

He focused on delivery pressures without auditing who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes. He also did not verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been masked or scrubbed from downstream environments, and he had not implemented compensating controls such as data masking or email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They worked collectively to understand what had happened and implement corrective controls. The root causes were insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed.

The client nevertheless demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt describes that as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” Afterward, IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.

🐾 Here’s a time Matt failed, with consequences for both customers and a teammate.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases. Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup, but he relied on the existing documentation instead of verifying that the controls were correct.

He focused on delivery pressures without auditing who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes. He also did not verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been masked or scrubbed from downstream environments, and he had not implemented compensating controls such as data masking or email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They worked collectively to understand what had happened and implement corrective controls. The root causes were insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed.

The client nevertheless demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt describes that as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” Afterward, IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.

🐾 Here’s how Matt built AWS Launchpad.

At **Accenture’s** Liquid Studio, traditional training programs couldn’t keep pace with rapidly evolving AWS technologies. Engineers had gaps in cloud competency, and cloud adoption was slowing. The Atlanta Innovation Hub needed a structured cloud enablement program that prepared engineers for cloud-native work, not just certification exams.

Matt led AWS Launchpad in collaboration with AWS, combining structured learning paths, hands-on labs, and mentor-based training. The program ran from July **2018** through November **2019**.

He designed learning paths and certification programs around AWS core services, including Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, Kubernetes, and ECS/Fargate, alongside cloud-native application development. Rather than relying on theory alone, he delivered interactive workshops and labs that immersed engineers in real-world AWS environments, reinforcing practical application.

Matt also established cloud expert mentorship teams to embed AWS best practices and build institutional knowledge. Group coaching sessions and knowledge-sharing workshops gave participants opportunities to learn together, with support extending beyond the individual training sessions. The program paired certification preparation with practical work and access to experienced cloud practitioners.

More than **200 professionals** earned AWS certifications, including AWS Solutions Architect and DevOps Engineer certifications. The program accelerated cloud adoption and the launch of cloud-native initiatives at **Accenture**, while establishing ongoing mentorship and knowledge-sharing practices for continued learning.
